title: Centrifuge cross-chain share transfers resolve the bridging contract from the counterparty's own vault at call time
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.6.5.5 resolves the transfer path through two hops of the counterparty's own contracts: "The operator must resolve the `spoke` contract that initiates the cross-chain transfer, obtained from the vault's async redeem `manager`" — implemented as `IAsyncRedeemManagerLike(ICentrifugeV3VaultLike(token).manager()).spoke()`.

This is a different trust posture from the rest of the controller. Bridge recipients are pinned in admin-only mappings (A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.1.1), pool parameters are admin-set, and venues are enabled by governance-written rate limits. Here the **contract that will actually execute the cross-chain send is discovered at call time from the vault**, so if Centrifuge changes its manager or spoke, Grove's transfer routes through the new contract with no governance action.

That is a reasonable engineering choice — hardcoding a counterparty's internal topology would break on every upgrade — but it means the integration's security depends on Centrifuge's own access control over `manager()` and `spoke()`, not only on Grove's.

Two guards remain in place. The **recipient** is still governance-pinned: A...2.6.5.4 requires `recipient != 0`, reverting with `centrifuge-id-not-configured`, so even a substituted spoke can only send to the address Grove's admin registered for that chain. And the rate limit still bounds the amount per token and destination.

The `payable` function forwarding `msg.value` as the messaging fee (A...2.6.5.1) is a further small departure: the relayer supplies ETH from outside the proxy to pay for the cross-chain message, so this operation has an external funding dependency the other controller functions do not.
description: The spoke that executes the transfer is read dynamically from the vault's async redeem manager rather than from governance configuration, and the relayer forwards the messaging fee as msg.value.
